name: w1
responses:
In genuinely high-speed threat environments, requiring a human to authorize every engagement could make defensive systems too slow to stop an incoming attack, potentially costing many lives. If a target has been independently validated as hostile and the system operates within strict, pre-approved rules, limited autonomous engagement can be justified.

This should be paired with strong safeguards—reliable identification, narrow mission scope, fail-safes, human oversight where feasible, and accountability—rather than granting weapons unrestricted autonomy.

Human authorization should prevail because lethal force involves contextual judgments—such as distinguishing civilians, assessing intent, and weighing escalation—that automated systems may not reliably make. Keeping a human accountable supports legal compliance, reduces the risk of mistaken or disproportionate attacks, and preserves meaningful political control over the use of force. Although this can impose reaction-time costs, those costs are generally preferable to delegating irreversible decisions to a system that may misinterpret rapidly changing circumstances.
